Monday. The history project was due Thursday. Vinita sent Imran her finished file at 9 p.m. "Just change the words a bit. Everyone does it."
Imran stared at it. It was good. His own was two paragraphs and a heading.
Tuesday. He didn't open her file again, though he kept thinking about it. He went to the library at lunch and found two books on the salt march. He wrote badly, crossed out, wrote again. At night he messaged Vinita, "Thanks, but I'll do mine."
"Your loss," she wrote.
Thursday. His project was shorter and messier than hers. But when Ma'am asked him a question about his sources, he could answer without looking. Walking out, he felt oddly light. Two other students' projects came back with "Please see me" on them.

qa.q: What did Imran find in the library at lunch?
qa.a: Two books on the salt march.

qa.q: How did Imran feel walking out on Thursday?
qa.a: Imran felt oddly light and relieved, because the work was his own and he could answer Ma'am's questions.

qa.q: Why does doing the work yourself matter here, even if the result is messier?
qa.a: Because Imran actually learned the topic and could explain his sources; copied work would have looked better but left him unable to answer.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when she hears "Please see me" on other projects?
qa.a: Vinita might feel uneasy and worried, wondering whether sharing her file could get her in trouble too.

grounding: Shows a teen resisting the temptation to copy a friend's project over several days and seeing why original work matters.

Harish, you're asking why I won't just let an app write your essay. Sit, I'll tell you a thing.
When I was sixteen, there was a district essay prize. The topic was my own town. I found an old magazine article that said everything better than I could. I copied three paragraphs, changed a few words, and won second prize.
At the prize function, the judge, an old schoolteacher, asked me to talk about the river bit, the part I'd copied. I couldn't. I stood there, my face burning. She didn't shame me in public. She just looked at me, and that was worse.
The next week I went to her house and told her the truth. She said, "Write it again, your own way." I did. It was worse. But it was mine. That's why your Zeenat Khala is so strict about this.

qa.a: Young Zeenat felt ashamed and trapped, with a burning face, because she couldn't talk about words that weren't hers.

qa.a: Going to the judge's house to tell the truth mattered, because it let her take responsibility and rewrite the essay honestly.

qa.q: How might the old schoolteacher have felt when young Zeenat came to confess?
qa.a: The teacher was probably disappointed at first, but moved and respectful that the girl came back on her own.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting a copied essay and why original work matters, as a lesson against AI shortcuts.

At 10:40 p.m., with the English essay due at midnight on the school portal, the power went out in Vidya's building. Her laptop had 20% battery. She had one paragraph.
Gopika texted: "Just use the AI thing. Two minutes. Nobody can tell."
Vidya almost did. Her finger was on the app. Then she thought about how the essay was supposed to be about her own grandmother's village, and how no app knew that.
Instead she wrote fast, by the light of her phone, a shorter essay in her own words. At 11:50 she submitted it, three paragraphs instead of five. Then she emailed Ms Fernandes: "The power went out. I've submitted what I wrote myself. Could I add the last two paragraphs tomorrow?"
Ms Fernandes replied in the morning: "Yes. Thank you for being honest."

qa.a: Vidya felt tempted and stressed by the deadline, but uneasy that no app knew her grandmother's village.

qa.a: Gopika might be surprised that honesty worked out, and maybe feel a little uncomfortable about suggesting the shortcut.

Lalremsiami had volunteered to lead her class stall at the school science fair in Aizawl. She made a task chart: who builds, who explains, who brings materials. Raghav was supposed to bring the plywood base. He forgot. Twice.
She didn't shout. On Wednesday she asked him, "What's actually stopping you?" He admitted he didn't know where to get it. She paired him with Mr Lalthanga, the carpentry teacher, and Raghav came back proud, carrying the board himself.

Sachin, you think your accent will make them laugh at college? Let me tell you mine.
When I was sixteen, I came from our village near Chhapra to a hostel in Mumbai. The first day I said "hum" for "I", and the boys in my room laughed till they cried. So I stopped talking. For months I practised "main" in the mirror. When Maa called, I whispered Bhojpuri so nobody would hear.
Then at the hostel's cultural night, a senior sang a Bhojpuri folk song. The whole hall clapped. After, he came to me: "You're from Saran? Talk to me in our language, yaar, I miss it."
I realised I'd been hiding the thing I was proud of at home. Now I speak English at the office, Hindi with friends, Bhojpuri with Maa, loudly. Your Nitin Chacha changes languages ten times a day and is ashamed of none.

qa.q: What did the senior sing at the cultural night?
qa.a: A Bhojpuri folk song.

qa.q: How did young Nitin feel whispering Bhojpuri on the phone to Maa?
qa.a: Young Nitin felt ashamed and afraid of being laughed at, so he hid the language he loved.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Nitin's story, and why?
qa.a: The senior asking to speak Bhojpuri with him, because it showed his home language could be something to share, not hide.

qa.q: How might the senior have felt meeting young Nitin?
qa.a: The senior was probably homesick and delighted to find someone from the same region to speak with.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recalling how he moved from hiding his home language to switching proudly between cultures.

Yash was forty minutes into a live gaming stream with his friend Parveen, two hundred people watching, when his Ba walked in with a plate of thepla.
"Yash, khaai le, beta. Thandu thai jashe."
The chat exploded: "lol what language", "grandma cameo", "subtitles pls". Yash's ears went red. The game was at a crucial point; he had seconds to decide what to do.
He took the plate. "Thank you, Ba." Then, to the camera: "That's Gujarati. My Ba says eat before it gets cold. She's the real boss here."
Parveen laughed. "Ba, say hi!"
Ba waved at the screen, confused and delighted. The chat filled with "hi Ba", and someone asked for the thepla recipe.
After the stream Yash sat for a moment. He had expected to be mocked. Instead the clip with Ba got the most views.

qa.a: A plate of thepla.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the chat exploded?
qa.a: Yash felt embarrassed, with red ears, and worried he'd be mocked on stream.

qa.a: Explaining Ba's words proudly instead of hiding her made the moment warm, so viewers joined in rather than mocking.

qa.a: Ba was confused but delighted, probably happy to be greeted by her grandson's friends online.

Dear Salma,
Remember in Class 8, when you joined our school, I asked if people in Afghanistan lived in tents? You said, "Some do. My family had a flat with a balcony and a lemon tree," and walked off. I thought you were rude.

Akash

Lokesh, on your podcast you asked what changed my mind about migrants. It was my own Uppa.
I'm Nazia. My grandfather went from Kozhikode to Dubai at nineteen to work on building sites. I'd heard the family version: brave, successful, sent money home. But at school, I'd also laughed at jokes about the workers who come to our city from Bihar and Odisha.
For a school project I interviewed three of them at a construction site near our flat. One man, Manoj, showed me a photo of his daughter's school uniform. He said he sees her once a year.
That night I asked Uppa what Dubai was like. He was quiet, then said, "Lonely. People called us names." I realised the men I'd laughed at were living his story.
I don't laugh at those jokes anymore. I ask where people are from instead.

qa.a: He went from Kozhikode to Dubai to work on building sites.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel after Uppa said Dubai was lonely?
qa.a: Nazia felt shaken and ashamed, realising the workers Nazia had laughed at were living Uppa's story.

qa.q: What could other students learn from Nazia's project?
qa.a: Talking to people directly and connecting their stories to your own family can break down prejudice more than jokes or assumptions.

qa.a: Manoj may have felt respected and seen, sharing something personal like his daughter's photo.

I'm Wasim, and I sit two rows behind Vaibhav in our Bengaluru school.
When the two exchange students from Kenya arrived in November, Vaibhav whispered a joke about lions and running. Some of us laughed. I did too, I'm not proud of it.
Then in geography, the teacher asked them to present their city, Nairobi. They showed photos: tall buildings, traffic jams worse than ours, a mall, their school robotics lab. Vaibhav went very still.

In Osaka, the results for the high school entrance exam were posted online at 10 a.m. Aiko's number wasn't there. She checked three times.
She didn't cry until she reached the river path, where Kwame, her friend from the running club, found her.
"I studied every day for a year," she said. "My mother told everyone."
Kwame sat down. "My brother failed his first one too. He went to his second-choice school, and now he's at university."
"That's different."
"Maybe. But one exam isn't your whole life."
Aiko went home. Her mother hugged her before she said anything. That evening they looked at the second-choice school's brochure together. It had a strong science club. Aiko didn't feel happy. But for the first time that day, she felt something like hope.

qa.a: At 10 a.m.

qa.a: Aiko felt crushed and disappointed, and worried about letting her mother down after a year of studying.

qa.q: What helped Aiko begin to cope, and why?
qa.a: Kwame's story about a brother and her mother's hug without blame helped, and looking at a real next option gave her something to move toward.

qa.q: What was it like for Aiko's mother to see her daughter come home?
qa.a: Her mother was probably sad for Aiko but wanted her to feel loved first, which is why she hugged her before she said anything.

In the school counsellor's room, Hafsa sat with her hands tucked under her legs. Her father's shop had closed last month. She'd quietly dropped out of the school trip and stopped going to tuition, and she'd been walking her little brother Farhan home early to cook, because her mother was working longer shifts.
"I don't want anyone to know," she said. "Everyone will pity us."
The counsellor didn't push. She asked what Hafsa was worried about most. "Falling behind. And Farhan. He cries at night."
They made a plan: the school had a free study group after classes that Hafsa could join, and the counsellor would talk to Farhan's teacher, privately. She also asked if she could call Hafsa's mother. Hafsa nodded.
Walking out, Hafsa still felt heavy. But lighter than when she'd come in.

qa.q: What happened to Hafsa's father's shop?
qa.a: It closed last month.

qa.a: Hafsa felt ashamed and afraid of being pitied by others.

qa.a: She asked what worried Hafsa most, offered a free study group and private support for Farhan, and asked permission before calling her mother.

qa.a: Farhan might get gentle support at school and feel less alone, which could help with crying at night.

I'm Pallavi, and I've sat next to Joseph since Class 9.
At first I thought he was just dramatic. The assembly bell would ring and he'd flinch and cover his ears. In the canteen, he'd eat fast and leave. Once, during a fire drill, he went pale and stood very still in the corridor while everyone else ran.
In Class 10 he did something I didn't expect. He went to our class teacher and asked, calmly, if he could sit near the door, use soft earplugs in the canteen and during drills, and leave assembly a minute early. He explained that loud sudden sounds feel much bigger to him than to others.
She agreed. After that he seemed calmer, answered more in class, and even joined the quiz team.
I can't know exactly what it's like for him. But I stopped calling it dramatic.

qa.a: To sit near the door, use soft earplugs in the canteen and during drills, and leave assembly a minute early.

qa.q: What could other students with sensory sensitivity learn from Joseph?
qa.a: Noticing what overwhelms you and asking calmly for specific changes can make school much easier.

Teacher's note. Kavitha, geography, Eco Club supervisor.
Urmila came to the Eco Club overwhelmed after a news report on melting glaciers. "What's the point? We're just kids."
I asked her to first explain the cause to the club: burning coal, petrol and diesel releases gases that trap heat, like a blanket that keeps getting thicker. She did, with a chart. That seemed to calm her.
Then I asked, "What's one thing our school burns fuel for?" The club listed: generator, school buses, parents' cars at pick-up.
Urmila proposed a "walk or cycle Wednesday" for students within two kilometres and a check of how long the generator runs. She surveyed the classes herself.
Results after a month: forty students joining Wednesdays. It's not saving the world, as she said. But she's stopped saying "what's the point".

qa.q: What did the Eco Club list that the school burns fuel for?
qa.a: The generator, school buses and parents' cars at pick-up.

qa.q: How was Urmila feeling when she came to the club?
qa.a: Urmila felt overwhelmed and hopeless after the news report on melting glaciers.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha's approach help Urmila?
qa.a: Understanding the cause first calmed her, and finding one local, realistic action turned hopelessness into something she could do.

qa.q: How might the forty students on Wednesdays see Urmila's idea?
qa.a: They might enjoy it and feel part of something useful, even if it's small.

grounding: Shows a teen learning the causes of climate change and organising a realistic group action at school.

Diary, Aparna here. It was 45 degrees today. School cut the afternoon classes. Ira and I walked home under one umbrella and still felt like we were melting.

passage:
Week 1: Anjali decided to start running with her brother Karthik before school. Five minutes in, she was gasping and walked home. Karthik didn't laugh, just said, "Tomorrow, same time."
Week 3: She'd kept going, but slowly: run one minute, walk one minute, for twenty minutes. Some mornings she hated it. She also noticed she was starving afterwards and started eating a proper breakfast, eggs and a banana, instead of skipping it for the bus.
Week 6: On a cool Sunday, she ran the whole park loop without stopping. Karthik was behind her, for once.
She didn't feel like an athlete. But she felt steadier in class, and she was sleeping better. She pinned a calendar to her wall and put a tick on every running day.

qa.q: What did Anjali start eating for breakfast?

qa.q: How did Anjali feel after running the whole park loop?
qa.a: Anjali felt steadier and quietly proud, even if she didn't feel like an athlete.

qa.q: Which habit helped most, and why?

qa.q: How might Karthik feel seeing her ahead of him in week 6?

passage:
Pallavi, you want to train two hours every day from tomorrow? I did that once. Listen.
I was fifteen, Sahil the skinny one. A new gym opened near our house. I decided to become strong in a month. First week, I lifted every day, skipped rest, ate only eggs. By day nine my shoulder hurt so badly I couldn't lift my school bag. The doctor said to rest, and I sat out for three weeks, angry and sulking.
My coach at the time said, "Strong is built like a wall. One brick a day, not all at once."
So I started again, slowly. Three days a week. Dal, rice, vegetables, not just eggs. Sleep. It took a year. But I never stopped again.
That's why your Sahil Mama will make you start with twenty minutes.

qa.q: What happened to young Sahil's shoulder by day nine?
qa.a: It hurt so badly that young Sahil couldn't lift the school bag.

qa.q: How did young Sahil feel sitting out for three weeks?
qa.a: Young Sahil felt angry and frustrated, sulking about the lost time.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sahil's story, and why?
qa.a: Starting again slowly, three days a week with balanced meals, because steady habits lasted where rushing had failed.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt watching young Sahil come back?
qa.a: The coach was probably relieved and pleased that the boy had learned patience rather than quitting.

grounding: Shows an elder recounting how rushed training failed and consistent fitness and eating habits worked.

passage:
Yusuf had played football every evening until his Class 12 boards started. Now there was no time, the family's flat was one room and a kitchen, and the park was far.
He felt sluggish and snappish. His mother, Sangeeta, noticed him snacking on chips at midnight.
"You used to be happy after football," she said.
"No time, Ammi. No space."
They worked it out together. Fifteen minutes every morning before study: skipping rope on the roof, push-ups and squats beside the bed. Water bottle on the desk. Fruit instead of chips for the late-night hunger, and dinner a little later so he wasn't starving.
The first week he missed three days. The second, only one. By the end of the month, he wasn't as snappish, and his notes looked tidier. "Fifteen minutes is nothing," he said. "But it's not nothing."

qa.q: What did Yusuf do on the roof each morning?
qa.a: He did skipping rope.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel before the new routine?
qa.a: Yusuf felt sluggish and snappish, missing the football that used to make him happy.

qa.q: What made the plan work despite little time and space?
qa.a: Keeping it short and at the same time daily, using the roof and bedside, and swapping chips for fruit made it easy to stick to.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel by the end of the month?
qa.a: Sangeeta probably feels relieved and pleased to see her son calmer and more focused.

grounding: Illustrates a teen keeping a consistent fitness and eating routine under exam-time and space constraints.

passage:
Lakshmi, you asked what the philosophy club was like. I'm Anirban, and I went because of a free samosa, but I stayed because of one question.
The teacher asked: "If a friend asks if their drawing is good and it's terrible, do you lie?" We split into groups. One side argued the way some thinkers do: do whatever makes the most people happy, so be kind. Another side said lying is wrong in itself, no matter what. My friend Deepa brought up the Buddhist idea of right speech, truthful but also kind and timely. Our coach pointed out we'd found three different systems in one room.
What surprised me was nobody was stupid. Each view had a reason. I used to think religions and philosophies were just teams to support. Now I think they're tools, and you compare them fairly before you pick one up.

qa.q: What question did the teacher ask the club?
qa.a: "If a friend asks if their drawing is good and it's terrible, do you lie?"

qa.q: Why did Anirban feel surprised by the discussion?
qa.a: Anirban felt surprised and impressed that each view had a reason and nobody was stupid.

qa.q: How could Anirban use what Anirban learned in a real disagreement?
qa.a: Anirban could lay out each side's reasons fairly before judging, rather than treating views as teams.

qa.q: How might Deepa have felt bringing a Buddhist idea to the group?
qa.a: Deepa may have felt glad and valued that the group treated the idea as one serious option among others.

grounding: Shows a teen comparing ethical systems and a religious teaching reasonably in a philosophy club.

passage:
I'm Chinmay. I was at Anirban's house during Durga Puja when he got into it with his grandmother about karma.
He'd been reading about atheism and said, "Thamma, there's no proof of past lives." I braced for a fight. She just put down her tea. "Then how do you explain why good people suffer?"
Anirban started to argue, then stopped. He asked her instead, "What does karma mean to you, really?" She talked for twenty minutes, about her own mother, about fairness over lifetimes. He listened without interrupting.
Then he explained why he doubted it, calmly, and she listened too.
Nobody changed their mind. But when I left, they were still talking, and she was laughing. I don't know what he was thinking. But he looked curious, not smug.

qa.q: What was Anirban's grandmother drinking?
qa.a: She was drinking tea, which she put down.

qa.q: What does Anirban stopping mid-argument suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Anirban felt curious and a bit humbled, deciding understanding her mattered more than winning.

qa.q: What approach made this disagreement respectful?
qa.a: Each asked the other what the belief meant to them and listened fully before explaining their own view.

qa.q: How might Thamma have felt being asked to explain karma?
qa.a: Thamma likely felt respected and happy that her grandson wanted to understand rather than mock.

grounding: Illustrates, through an observer, a teen comparing a religious belief and a non-religious view reasonably with a grandparent.

passage:
Monday, logic class. Hansa said, "All religions teach the same thing: be good." Irawati said, "That sounds nice, but is it true?" The teacher smiled and asked them to test it by Friday.
Wednesday, library. They made a chart: ideas about God, about the afterlife, about how to live, from five traditions plus two non-religious philosophies. Some overlapped a lot, like kindness and honesty. Some didn't at all: one god, many gods, no god; one life or many. Hansa frowned. "So I was wrong?"
"Half right," Irawati said. "The ethics overlap more than the beliefs."
Friday, they presented. Hansa said, "I wanted it to be simple because simple feels peaceful. But respecting them means seeing they're different." The class was quiet. Then the teacher said, "That's the best conclusion anyone's reached this term."

qa.q: What did Hansa and Irawati put in their chart?
qa.a: Ideas about God, the afterlife and how to live, from five traditions plus two non-religious philosophies.

qa.q: Why did Hansa want all religions to teach the same thing?
qa.a: Hansa wanted it to be simple because simple felt peaceful, and Hansa felt unsettled when the chart showed real differences.

qa.q: Which part of their method was fair, and why?
qa.a: Comparing several traditions and philosophies side by side on the same questions, so claims were checked rather than assumed.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel hearing Hansa's conclusion?
qa.a: Irawati would probably feel pleased and proud that their work led Hansa to a more honest view.

grounding: Shows teens reasoning carefully over a week to compare religions and philosophies instead of oversimplifying.

passage:
In Lagos, Amara had four months to learn one song on guitar for the school's end-of-year concert. Her cousin Nadia had lent her the guitar and a chord sheet.
The first week was exciting. By the fifth, her fingers hurt and the same chord change sounded awful every single time. She was bored of the song before she could play it.
Nadia suggested something: a calendar with a small square for every day she practised, even ten minutes. "Don't count hours. Count squares."
Some days Amara only managed the ten minutes. Some days the power was out and she practised without an amp in the dark. In month three, the chord change finally clicked.
At the concert her hands shook. She got through the whole song. Afterwards she looked at her calendar: ninety-one squares.

qa.q: How many squares did Amara count on her calendar after the concert?
qa.a: Ninety-one squares.

qa.q: How did Amara feel in the fifth week?
qa.a: Amara felt bored and discouraged, with sore fingers and a chord change that sounded awful every time.

qa.q: Why did Nadia's calendar idea help?
qa.a: Counting days instead of hours made small, steady practice feel like progress, even on bad days.

qa.q: How might Nadia feel watching Amara play at the concert?
qa.a: Nadia would probably feel proud and happy that the lent guitar and the calendar idea helped.

grounding: Illustrates a teen sustaining practice over months despite boredom and setbacks.

passage:
For the science exhibition, Zeenat's group had to grow bean plants for three months under different kinds of light. Their teacher, Rekha Ma'am, had warned them: "Long projects are boring in the middle."
Month one was fun. Month two, Zeenat was the only one still coming to water them on Saturdays. Then the lab's fan broke over a hot weekend and half the plants died.
Zeenat sat on the lab floor, nearly in tears. Rekha Ma'am sat with her. "What do you still have?"
"Half the plants. And my notes."
"Then that's data too. Why did some survive?"
Zeenat rewrote the plan. She made a rota so everyone watered once a week, and added a new question: which light helped plants survive heat. At the exhibition, their stall had the most questions from judges.

qa.q: What happened to the plants over the hot weekend?
qa.a: The lab's fan broke and half the plants died.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling on the lab floor?
qa.a: Zeenat felt devastated and discouraged, nearly in tears after months of care.

qa.q: Which of Rekha Ma'am's questions turned the setback around, and why?
qa.a: "What do you still have?" helped, because it turned the loss into data and a new question to explore.

qa.q: How might the other group members see the new rota?
qa.a: They may feel a bit guilty for dropping off, but more committed now they share the work.

grounding: Shows a teen sustaining a multi-month project through boredom and a setback with a teacher's help.
